passage:
Monday, 7:40 pm. Reena had meant to message alumni for three weeks. Every evening she argued with herself: too tired, too early, too awkward. She wrote a rule on a card: When the clock hits eight on a work night, two alumni get a message before supper.
Tuesday, eight o'clock. The alarm buzzed. She felt the usual pull to put it off, but the rule had already decided. She opened her list: two names, two short messages, sent in twelve minutes.
Thursday of the next week. Santosh, a senior at a mid-sized firm, replied: “Happy to chat on Saturday.” By then, sending had stopped feeling like a choice. It was simply what happened at eight.

qa.a: Santosh, a senior at a mid-sized firm, replied.

qa.q: How does Reena feel when the alarm buzzes on Tuesday?
qa.a: Reena feels the usual pull to put it off, but the rule has already decided, so she starts anyway.

qa.q: What could Reena do if a work night is impossible?
qa.a: Reena could set a backup time, such as a weekend morning, keeping the same if-then form so nothing is left to argue about.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel getting the message?
qa.a: Santosh is probably glad to be asked and happy to help, since the reply offers a chat on Saturday.

grounding: The student writes an if-then rule to send two messages to alumni at a fixed time, which removes the daily debate about whether to start.
